raw_response.overlap_rationale: Both full texts are accessible and authored by Maria Rusca (with different co-author teams) studying urban water supply in Lilongwe, Malawi (Lilongwe Water Board network and kiosks), but they draw on completely non-overlapping fieldwork periods, distinct datasets, and different analytical designs. Study A (Rusca et al. 2015) examines institutional bricolage and elite capture in WaterAid-supported Water Users Associations (WUAs) using fieldwork conducted from November 2008 to February 2009 and November 2013 to January 2014 (48 semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and 30 household questionnaires). Study B (Rusca et al. 2017) examines physicochemical and microbiological drinking water quality inequalities across Lilongwe's centralized water network using later fieldwork conducted between September/November 2014 and February 2015 and February to April 2016 under the UNHIDE and Horizon 2020 INHAbIT Cities projects (80 interviews, the March-April 2016 UNHIDE-INHAbIT survey of n = 497 households across six administrative areas, and 170 laboratory water samples from Areas 2, 7, 47 and 56). Because data collection waves, samples, and outcomes are empirically distinct, there is no shared sample or double-counting risk.
raw_response.study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative and small-N mixed-methods case study of WaterAid-initiated Water Users Associations (WUAs) in peri-urban Lilongwe, Malawi (including Chinsapo, Mtandire/Mtsiliza, Kauma, Area 50, Mgona, Chimutu III, Tsabango, Area 24, Area 41). Fieldwork conducted November 2008–February 2009 and November 2013–January 2014: N = 48 semi-structured interviews (WaterAid London and Malawi staff, Lilongwe Water Board/KMU officials, WUA representatives, key informants), focus group discussions (WUAs, CBOs, NGO partners), and N = 30 semi-structured household consumer questionnaires.
raw_response.study_b_sample_and_data: Interdisciplinary mixed-methods political ecology and water-quality study of Lilongwe Water Board's centralized water network in Lilongwe, Malawi (UNHIDE and Horizon 2020 INHAbIT Cities projects). Fieldwork conducted September/November 2014–February 2015 and February–April 2016: N = 80 interviews (urban planners, LWB managers/staff, MBS, kiosk attendants, residents), UNHIDE-INHAbIT household survey of n = 497 in six administrative areas (March–April 2016), and laboratory microbiological/physicochemical analysis (E. coli, total coliforms, turbidity, free/total chlorine) of N = 170 water samples from two low-income areas (Area 56, Area 7) and two higher-income areas (Area 47, Area 2).
